snippet.textDisplay: When my mother had a heart attack at 86, she was already suffering from numerous health issues, could barely walk, and needed help (I lived in my parent's home at the time)  with almost everything. Her cardiologist did not think she was a good surgical candidate for a stent, and placed her on medication instead. Enter my sister, who demanded she have surgery and asked for the person in charge (at the hospital). The stent has given her almost 4 more years of even worse health issues, and the assisted living facility I had to place her in is almost $10K/month for her rent and care. If she had a quality of life post stent I would have been all for the surgery, but her cardiologist was right all along. And even with assisted living you still have to be present and involved, do supply runs, etc. My mother will be 90 in July, and my anxiety is always through the roof! She's on at least three pages of medications. Without them, I'm sure she would have passed much earlier.

snippet.textDisplay: My mom passed away 5 months ago.  I moved back home 15 years ago to care for my mom when my dad died.  After 8 years I retired to care for my mom full time.  In her last 7 years, because she was housebound, I never left the house.  I shopped once per month for 60 minutes and went to Sunday Mass for 45 minutes weekly.  I never asked for help from anyone.  Those 15 years, especially the last 7 years, were the 7 best years of my life.  I did everything for my mom and thank God that He gave me the grace to care for my mom.  There is nothing in this world that I would trade those last 7 years for.  I never saw it to be a burden.  I loved my mom so much that, 5 months now after she passed away, my heart is still broken and desolate.  I never saw it as stressful, unbearable, etc.  I did everything out of love.  If it were my choice, I would have done it for another 50 years.  My mom passed at 101.  I pray she is now in Heaven with God.

snippet.textDisplay: What a great initiative . I am writing from India where we are expected to look after our parents at home . There are no hospice or care homes , may be one or two . It is considered shameful to put parents in  care home . snippet.textDisplay: I am a 49 year old male who looks after my 90 year old mother who has vascular dementia. I quit work to be her full time carer. I am entirely alone - I have no siblings and my relatives say that they don't care about me as I am not a member of their immediate family. I often feel burnt out and stressed out but I wouldn't change it for anything. My mother looked after me for the first 42 years of my life so there is no way that I will ever let her go into a nursing home. After a stay in hospital, the hospital refused to let her come back home with me (I found out that they did this to every elderly patient on the ward, they had an 'arrangement' with a nursing home) . They dumped her in a nursing home - but I used my Power of Attorney to rescue her and get her back home with me. She was always there for me growing up so I am here for her. Everybody remember this - you may feel frustrated now but one day your loved ones will be gone and you would do anything and give away everything you have for just one more moment with them - so cherish them now. Don't grumble or be resentful - do it with a smile on your face and thank God that they are still here. Which would you rather be doing? - working for some bastard of a boss in an office or looking after the person who cared for you and gave you life? At the end of the day there is nothing more meaningful. To be honest, if I had children and they wanted to put me in a home I would feel completely betrayed. If your children are going to abandon you at your time of desperate need then why bother having them? - it means all those years of raising them have amounted to absolutely nothing. I know that some people genuinely can't cope but many more just dump them because they can't be bothered and are just too selfish. Looking after your elderly parents is a privilege, it really is. Any parents who are able to still make decisions - cut the buggers out of your will if they don't look after you!

snippet.textDisplay: I've noticed this myself.  THANK YOU for your years of service working with the elderly.  I've had several family members in nursing homes including my mother with Alzheimer's.  We managed to keep her at home until about 18 months before she passed.  Most people have completely unrealistic expectations of the level of care nursing homes can provide.  They think because the care is expensive, that nursing homes can afford to have someone waiting by their bedsides every hour of the day and night.  They seem think that people are lining up outside the doors for a chance to work in this challenging environment when the exact opposite is true.  It's a very tough job that no one wants to do because of the low pay and high stress.  Most facilities struggle to remain financially solvent due to the fact that most residents are on Medicaid and the reimbursement rates often don't cover the costs.  People complain when nursing homes close due to insolvency, but refuse to pay higher taxes to keep them adequately funded.

That happens so often and it’s incredibly frustrating. People with dementia can “perform” for a few minutes, and professionals sometimes miss what’s really going on. If it’s safe to do, consider video recording short clips of the aggressive or confused behavior. It can be really helpful to show the full picture to doctors, social workers, or senior services.

For help, you can contact your local Area Agency on Aging go to Eldercare.acl.gov and enter your ZIP code to find resources near you. You can also ask your parent’s doctor for a referral to a neurologist or geriatric specialist for a full cognitive evaluation. You deserve support and you’re not alone in this. You are right too that it will only get worse. Hang in there.
